title: Dasharatha's sacrifice
hook: a city where everyone is content, and the one man in it who isn't

segments.voice: Yesterday: the crow and the first verse, and Brahma's promise. As long as mountains stand, Rama's story will be told, and two boys learned it by heart.

The first thing Valmiki gives us is a city. Ayodhya, on the river Sarayu, in the land of Kosala. Wide straight roads sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers, gates and arches, music, merchants, horses, elephants, full granaries. In his telling, nobody there is greedy, nobody lies, nobody is without learning or without food. A city working as it should. And at its center sits a king who has everything, and who can't sleep for wanting the one thing he doesn't have.
screen: `AYODHYA, ON THE SARAYU.` → `A CITY WORKING AS IT SHOULD.` → `A KING WHO CAN'T SLEEP.`

segments.voice: The king is Dasharatha, of the line of Ikshvaku. His name means ten chariots, and tradition explains it as one whose chariot could go in all ten directions. He's wise, generous, a famous warrior, guided by great counselors like the sage Vasishtha. He has three chief queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And he has no son. For a king in the epic's world, that isn't only personal sorrow. It's the line, the ancestors' rites, the kingdom's future. So Dasharatha thinks it through and decides: I will perform the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice, for the sake of sons. Notice how he does it. He doesn't act alone. He calls his priests and ministers, lays out his grief and his plan, and asks. They approve. Then his charioteer and counselor, Sumantra, takes him aside with a story. Long ago, he says, he heard sages foretell this very moment: a king of Ikshvaku's line, longing for sons, would bring a certain young sage to his sacrifice, and sons would come. The sage's name is Rishyashringa, and his story is strange enough to take all of tomorrow. So the Ramayana's first real scene isn't heroic at all. It's a good man with everything, admitting what he lacks to the people around him, and asking for help.
screen: `DASHARATHA: TEN CHARIOTS.` · `THREE QUEENS, AND NO SON.` · `HE ASKS HIS COUNSELORS FIRST.` · `SUMANTRA REMEMBERS A PROPHECY.` · then, large: `THE HORSE SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Let one longing come up, something you've wanted a long time and don't have, and hold it honestly, without pushing it away or feeding it. Then bring to mind one person you trust, and simply notice they're there. Breathe with the longing and the company together.
Dasharatha's sacrifice. The great horse sacrifice the childless king of Ayodhya decides on, with his counselors, for the sake of sons.
Your line: admitting what he lacks. Even a king with everything had something missing. That's day four hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Ayodhya, on the Sarayu river in today's Uttar Pradesh, is revered in Hindu tradition as Rama's birthplace and is a place of pilgrimage; the Bala Kanda's opening chapters describe the city and its king.

myth: Dasharatha decides on the sacrifice without consulting anyone
he lays out his grief and plan to his priests and ministers first.
Sumantra links the moment to an old prophecy
a young sage named Rishyashringa will bring sons to the king.

fork.setup: you're Dasharatha. you have everything a king could want, except a son. what do you do?
options: decide on a great sacrifice, with your counselors' blessing.
go to war to win glory instead.
fork.reveal: he resolves on the ashvamedha for the sake of sons, and asks his priests and ministers first. they approve.

original.note: Sanskrit aśvamedha: the horse sacrifice, a great royal Vedic rite.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Ramayana begins with Rama.
what it means: it begins with his father's longing, admitted honestly, and a decision made with others.

what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 5–8 describe Ayodhya and Dasharatha's court before the decision for the ashvamedha; Sumantra then tells of Rishyashringa, citing a prophecy he attributes to the sage Sanatkumara.
guess: the horse rite the childless king holds for sons
a king's offering of thanks after a great victory
a fire rite to end a long drought in Ayodhya

chat.says: Why does the Ramayana start with a king planning a sacrifice?
options: He has everything but a son, so he asks his counselors and plans a rite for sons.
He has many sons already and wants the gods to make them famous and strong.
A curse forces him into it, and he goes ahead without asking anyone at all.
chat.meaning: Childless Dasharatha lays out his grief to his priests and ministers and decides on the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice, for the sake of sons.

Ayodhya.meaning: Dasharatha's city, on the river Sarayu

ashvamedha.meaning: the great horse sacrifice of ancient kings

Kausalya.meaning: one of Dasharatha's three chief queens

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 5–7 (Ayodhya, Dasharatha, his counselors)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 8–9 (the decision for the horse sacrifice; Sumantra's prophecy)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common vulgate numbering; the Critical Edition differs.
The meaning 'ten chariots' and its explanation (a chariot that goes in ten directions) is a traditional gloss; confirm.
Valmiki's idealized city (no greed, no lies, no one unlearned) paraphrased from Bala Kanda 6; confirm.
The prophecy Sumantra recalls is attributed to Sanatkumara in the vulgate; confirm.
